paragraphs: After the snowy night in Chang’an, many people on the official road north of Luoyang still had not made it home.

Soldiers discharged first lined up outside county gates to reclaim the knives and other belongings withheld when their units were dispersed, along with the road rations still owed them. The civilian porters who came later had no such settled procedure. Some possessed only a wooden token; others clutched labor vouchers whose seals were too faint to make out. The county clerks dared promise nothing. They entered surnames under the home villages, packing one register densely with names while the household totals in another stubbornly failed to agree.

Han Chong, the officer who had escorted the rear camp, often dreamed of the Fei River. On the day of the withdrawal the reeds along the bank had already yellowed, and the last soldiers dismantling the bridge were still on the northern shore. The ropes of the pontoon bridge were stiff with frost. When an iron hook was pulled free, it tore away a broad sheet of thin ice. The Jin watchtower across the river stood plainly in view. A Jin archer bent to pick up his quiver, moving as slowly as an ordinary woodcutter beside a stream.

Han Chong had counted the recovered bridge planks twice before ordering them loaded. He was supposed to cover the withdrawal of the rear camp, yet what arrived before him was one cart after another of timber to be entered back into the registers. Before they departed, a boy in his squad looked toward the southern bank and asked, “Are we truly not going to fight?”
“Do you want to go home and farm next year?” Han Chong asked.
The boy nodded.
“Then tie those planks down tight.”
The words were quiet, but they carried the authority of a marching order.

When these soldiers had gone south from Luoyang, they had looked up at their banners and talked of winning fame by breaking the enemy in battle. On their way north, they spent most of their time watching the ruts. The soundest roads were reserved for wagons carrying the wounded and sick; on steep slopes, horses least able to bear the cold were sent ahead. As illness spread through the traveling camp, even the midnight change of guard was made without beating drums or striking gongs, lest the newly sleeping wounded be roused.

By the time the convoy reached the country north of Xuchang, broken wagon wheels lay heaped by the roadside like doors stripped from abandoned houses. Liang Cheng, a civilian porter, sat beside a ditch shaping a piece of elmwood with a broken blade. His right shoulder had once been dislocated; raising it too high brought a piercing pain. Still, he refused to leave the convoy. A squad leader from Hedong asked him, “There’s no military glory in it for you. Why stay?”
“What else would I do? Mend the wheels.”
“Wouldn’t you rather go home and collect your pay?”
Liang Cheng held a wood shaving between his teeth and muttered, “If the carts don’t move, no one gets paid.”

His father was Di; his mother came from a Han family. As a boy in the garrison town he had learned to speak the Di language, and after marrying he followed the Han seasonal rites of his village. Whenever the county authorities called for labor service, they liked to ask which people he belonged to, as though writing either Di or Han beside his name would somehow alter the reckoning of his labor dues.

On this campaign Liang Cheng had been entered in the labor rolls of the rear army at Xuchang. He first accompanied the Luoyang wagons, then was sent to repair bridges at Runan, and finally pulled out wooden piles from the northern bank of the Fei. In the five or six handwritten registers, his name appeared sometimes as Liang Cheng, sometimes with a different character for Cheng. He did not know enough characters to argue. Only when he went to claim his voucher for the journey home did he discover that more than half the road he had traveled had vanished from his record.

He waited all day in the snow with a group of porters. When the registration shed’s wooden noticeboard was taken down, the men began shouting in alarm. The clerk issuing vouchers tucked his hands into his sleeves and told them across the desk, “Today we verify only Xuchang’s main roll. The rest must come back tomorrow.”

“I’ve been here three times already.” Liang Cheng placed the half-finished wooden axle on the desk. “Your main roll says I stayed in Xuchang forty-nine days. Who counted the days when I went to Runan?”
“Ask Runan,” the clerk said impatiently.
“Runan told me to come to Xuchang.”

Behind him, a Qiang porter grew so anxious that he began explaining in his native speech. The clerk could not understand a word. The light faded, but the crowd outside the shed refused to disperse. Someone quietly began piling dry sticks by the road, intending to sit watch beside the desk all night.

A mounted grain escort now approached from the north. Seeing several hundred people blocking the military gate, the officer in command thought a mutiny was beginning and immediately ordered his soldiers forward. Liang Cheng rose, felt a stab in his shoulder, and almost fell. The officer recognized the number of his former unit and told his men to lower their halberds.
“Who is in charge of this group?”
The squad leaders looked at one another before finally pointing to Liang Cheng.
“He kept the wagons running all the way here.”

The officer crouched to examine the half-cut axle and asked Liang Cheng at which bridges he had changed the wheels. Pointing toward the frozen watercourse ahead, Liang named the shallows, wooden bridges, and sinking slopes one by one. He even remembered the day a gray mule was lost. The officer then ordered the clerk to fetch the grain tokens issued to the convoy at various points along the road. The old numbers on those tokens matched the sequence of wagons Liang Cheng described.
“Write down the missing days in the margin for now,” the officer said. “Disputed entries can be checked tomorrow. Tonight the men can go warm themselves by the fire.”
The clerk was about to object that there was no county seal when the officer tapped the desk. “I marched that road myself. Will you write it or not?”
The clerk had no choice but to lift his brush. Liang Cheng’s name was provisionally entered in a column, with four small characters beside it: Travel service pending verification.
Liang Cheng would not leave. “Will those words buy me grain?”
“If they are verified tomorrow, they will.”
“And if you still cannot find the proof tomorrow?”
The officer paused. “Then we keep looking. Better than calling you a deserter tonight.”

Only then did Liang Cheng tuck the wooden axle into his sleeve. He offered no words of thanks. He was thinking merely of coming earlier the next morning, so he would not again stand in line until dark.
Outside Luoyang, the camps were also counting their men.

More than fifty thousand porters and craftsmen had gathered with the hundred and fifty thousand combat troops first assembled at Luoyang. Drivers, woodcutters, and road workers rotated in for short periods from provinces along the route and were recorded separately. Some served ten days in one place; others were borrowed again and again by different military offices, remaining in service for more than half a year. The farther the camps dispersed, the harder it became to bring the accounts together.

The army ordered departing soldiers to return public crossbows and long spears. One squad leader, however, hid thirty crossbow mechanisms beneath his bedboards, intending to sell them by night to a Luoyang smith. Of the eighty-seven soldiers who had left with him, just over seventy had returned. The others had died of illness, drowned along the road, or fallen behind and not reappeared. Asked why he meant to sell the weapons, he replied only, “I do not want to face their parents empty-handed.”

The officer holding him in custody was reluctant to pass sentence. Under military law, selling regulation crossbow mechanisms was a grave crime; according to the prisoner’s account, fifteen families still awaited relief. When the papers reached Fu Rong, he had just returned from inspecting grain stores in the camps, frost still caught in his hair. He wrote not a single word of leniency upon the charge, but beneath it added several lines: Verify each death and disappearance separately; issue vouchers to families whose relief remains unpaid; the outcome of the weapons case must neither be made conditional on relief payments nor used as a bargaining counter for them.
“The man will die,” an accompanying staff officer murmured.
“He hid military crossbows,” Fu Rong replied.
“What of the money he meant to send to the families?”
“Investigate it. Whoever is owed payment must receive it according to the records.”
“They will call Your Lordship heartless throughout the army.”
Fu Rong held the case papers and watched the men in the distance waiting to surrender their weapons. After a while he said, “Someone must bear their anger.”

The case was eventually sent to the Court of Justice for trial under the law. No sentence had yet been fixed, and the squad leader was not executed at the camp gate. Yet on the day the crossbows were collected, everyone saw the clerks count the thirty mechanisms in public, not one missing. Soldiers in line lowered their eyes, unsure whether they hoped the man would be spared or the military law would never change.

Day by day the winter wind sharpened. On the roads from Runan and Xuchang toward Guanzhong, returning men dragged broken wooden chests, old fragments of armor, and saved dry rations, traveling north in groups. Some had been left with a cough after illness and woke from sleep at the sound of hooves in the night. Others cursed the emperor for shrinking from battle, then sat down to mend a companion’s shoes.

The authorities continued checking unpaid accounts under the new court orders. Officials sent from Chang’an discovered one county had reported the destruction of the same civilian wagon three times, while in another they found a death register never submitted to the army office. Names long locked away in cupboards were copied out again. Women led their children past the county gates counting the seal impressions on their wooden vouchers as they walked, afraid they would once more be told they lacked a required formality.
One day in the twelfth month, Liang Cheng finally received his voucher.

Before the registration shed he took off his ragged robe and exposed the old injury on his right shoulder. A military physician felt along the bones and said the joint had been badly set; Liang would probably never again carry heavy loads. Liang Cheng laughed. “Then I won’t. I want to go home and make carts.”

The verifying officer compared the old records from Xuchang, Runan, and the Fei River, entered his days of labor, his injury, and the grain and money due him, and authorized one member of his household to be exempted from labor service the following year. Beside him a clerk asked out of habit, “People of origin?”
Liang Cheng looked up.
“My father was Di. My mother was Han.”
The clerk frowned, trying to choose between the two columns. The officer glanced at the military office’s register of verified payments. “On what grounds is grain issued?”
“Name, home registration, days of service, and injuries.”
“Then enter those. If another register requires ancestry, let the officials there verify it themselves.”

Liang Cheng turned the wooden voucher over and over in his hands. It bore neither of the two words he had been asked about all his life. Only the line of his name, which he had long ago learned to recognize, and a fresh dark-red seal.
Outside the shed a man from his village asked, “How much did you get?”
Liang Cheng named the amount. The other man did not believe him, saying that someone without battle honors could never receive so much. So Liang held out the voucher.
“Who did you fight?”
“No one.”
“They pay you even when you did no fighting?”
Liang Cheng looked at his stiff right shoulder and suddenly felt anger rise. “I spent a hundred and eighty-seven days on that road. What do you think I was doing?”

The man asked no more. They walked for a while and came upon a small salt wagon sunk into a shallow ditch at the roadside. Its owner called several times for help. Liang Cheng tucked the voucher securely away, but still went first to examine the wheel hub. With one hand he steadied the shafts and told the driver to unload two sacks of salt and find a stone to raise the axle.

Once the cart was free, its owner offered Liang Cheng a few coins. He waved them away and went west. Beneath the snow, homebound travelers had trampled two black tracks of mud into the official road. He followed the ruts, thinking of the broken waterwheel at home and whether he might still make it back for the spring planting. The wooden voucher rested against his chest. The seal was dry now. His name remained.
